question: How many air conditioning packs does the A320 family have, and what normally feeds each one?

options.text: Two packs; both are fed from the APU bleed in flight and from the engines only on the ground
Three packs, one per cabin zone, each fed by its own bleed duct
Two packs; pack 1 is fed from the left engine bleed and pack 2 from the right engine bleed
One pack per engine plus a third emergency pack fed by ram air

explanation: Each pack is supplied by the bleed system on its own side in the normal configuration. The cross bleed valve can link the two sides, which is how one engine bleed can feed both packs.

question: What is the job of the pack flow control valve?

options.text: It regulates the amount of bleed air entering the pack and closes to isolate the pack when required
It regulates the temperature of the air leaving the pack by mixing in hot air
It lets cabin air recirculate back through the pack
It controls how much ram air flows through the heat exchangers

explanation: Flow control is the valve's job; temperature is controlled elsewhere (the bypass valve and the ram air flap). The valve is electrically controlled and pneumatically operated.

question: What are the three positions of the PACK FLOW selector, and what do they do?

options.text: OFF, AUTO and MAN, which change who controls the packs
COLD, NORM and HOT, which change the target pack outlet temperature
ECON, NORM and MAX, which change the engine bleed stage used
LO, NORM and HI, which change the pack flow relative to normal

explanation: The selector only changes flow, never temperature. LO gives less flow than normal (around 80%), HI more (around 120%).

question: Approximately what pack flow do the LO and HI positions give compared with NORM?

options.text: About 50% for LO and about 150% for HI
About 80% for LO and about 120% for HI
About 90% for LO and about 110% for HI
LO and HI both give 100%; only the flow schedule changes

explanation: NORM is the reference, LO is roughly four fifths of it and HI roughly one fifth more. LO is used for a lightly loaded cabin to save fuel, HI to cool a full one.

question: When is HI pack flow selected automatically, regardless of the selector?

options.text: Whenever the aircraft is above FL250
When a single pack is operating, and when the packs are supplied by the APU bleed
Whenever both engine bleeds are operating
Only during the take-off roll to protect against engine bleed loss

explanation: With one pack lost, the remaining pack must supply the whole cabin, so the flow is raised automatically. The same applies when the APU is the bleed source.

question: Which flow setting should be considered when the cabin is lightly loaded, to reduce bleed demand?

options.text: HI
NORM with one pack off
HI, with the cross bleed valve closed
LO

explanation: A lightly loaded cabin needs less fresh air, so LO saves bleed air and therefore fuel. HI is used when the cabin is full or hot, or when only one pack is available.

question: What happens to a pack's flow control valve when its engine start is selected?

options.text: It closes automatically so that the start is not penalised by the bleed demand
It opens fully to cool the engine bay
It stays open but the flow drops to LO
It transfers its supply to the APU bleed

explanation: During engine start, bleed air must go to the starter, so the pack valve closes and the pack goes off line. It reopens once the start is finished.

question: Which of these events closes a pack flow control valve automatically?

options.text: Selecting the PACK FLOW selector to LO
Selecting the RAM AIR pushbutton
Pressing the engine fire pushbutton on the same side
Moving the zone temperature selectors to COLD

explanation: A fire pushbutton shuts the bleed and the pack valve on that side. Ditching and a pack overheat also close it. Flow selection and temperature changes do not.

question: What does the DITCHING pushbutton do to the air conditioning system?

options.text: It opens the ram air inlet to ventilate the cabin
It shuts off only the cargo ventilation
It isolates the left pack and keeps the right pack running
It closes the pack flow control valves and the outflow valve, together with other openings in the fuselage lower skin

explanation: Ditching preparation seals the fuselage as far as possible so the aircraft floats longer. The pack valves, outflow valve and other skin openings are closed.

question: How is the temperature of the air leaving a pack primarily controlled?

options.text: By the pack flow selector, which sets the outlet temperature directly
By the pack controller, which acts on the bypass valve and the ram air flow through the heat exchangers
By the position of the outflow valve
By the recirculation fans' speed

explanation: The pack controller works out the demand from the zone controller and mixes hot bleed air around the cooling process with the bypass valve while the ram air flap sets the cooling.

question: In the pack's air cycle machine, what cools the air most strongly?

options.text: Evaporation of fuel in the wing tanks
Compression of the air in the compressor stage
Expansion of the air through a turbine, after it has already been cooled in the heat exchangers
Mixing it with cold cabin air in the mixer unit

explanation: The compressor raises pressure and temperature, the heat exchangers (cooled by ram air) take heat out, and the expansion through the turbine then drops the temperature sharply.

question: Which component removes the water from the air leaving the pack's turbine?

options.text: The water extractor (condenser)
The mixer unit
The hot air pressure regulating valve
The recirculation filter

explanation: Cooling the air to a low temperature condenses moisture, which the water extractor separates before the air enters the distribution system. Without it the ducts would fill with water and ice.

question: What is the purpose of the anti-ice valve inside a pack?

options.text: To stop ice forming in the water extractor by modulating warm air to keep the outlet above freezing
To heat the cabin during ground operations
To protect the pack against over-pressure
To prevent ram air inlet icing

explanation: The cold air leaving the turbine can carry water at a temperature low enough to freeze in the extractor; the anti-ice valve limits how cold it can get.

question: What does the pack overheat protection do?

options.text: It switches the pack to HI flow to cool it
It opens the ram air inlet fully and keeps the pack running
It closes the pack flow control valve and turns the pack off, with the PACK pushbutton FAULT light
It transfers the load to the other pack and keeps both running

explanation: An overheat means the pack's own cooling cannot cope, so the supply must be cut. The crew can try to reset it later once the pack has cooled.

question: What are the three temperature zones on an A320 cabin?

options.text: The cockpit, the passenger cabin and the cargo hold
The cockpit, the forward cabin and the aft cabin
Left, right and centre of the cabin
Cockpit, galley and lavatories

explanation: Each zone has its own temperature selector on the overhead panel and its own trim air valve. The cargo compartments are not temperature zones in the same sense.

question: What is the range of the cabin zone temperature selectors?

options.text: From 0 °C to 40 °C, with the middle at 20 °C
From 10 °C to 25 °C, with the middle at 15 °C
From 15 °C to 35 °C, with the middle at 28 °C
From about 18 °C to about 30 °C, with the middle position around 24 °C

explanation: The selectors are not calibrated to a precise value but the range of 18–30 °C is the commonly quoted one, with the mid position around 24 °C.

question: Which unit computes the target temperature for each zone and for the pack outlets?

options.text: The cabin pressure controller
The pack flow control valve
The zone controller
The flight management guidance computer

explanation: The zone controller compares the selected and actual temperatures of each zone and sends the demands to the pack controllers and the trim air valves.

question: What is the principle used to set the pack outlet temperature when the three zones want different temperatures?

options.text: The packs deliver air at the temperature the coolest-demanding zone needs, and trim air warms the others
The packs deliver the average of the three selected temperatures
The packs deliver the temperature selected for the cockpit
The packs deliver the temperature of the warmest zone and the others are cooled by recirculation

explanation: Trim air can only add heat; nothing downstream of the pack can cool the air again. So the pack makes air for the coldest need and trim air raises it where needed.

question: What do the trim air valves add to the air going to a zone?

options.text: Cold air from the ram air inlet
Recirculated cabin air at a controlled temperature
Hot air from the engine nacelle anti-ice duct
Hot bleed air, taken from upstream of the packs

explanation: Hot air is tapped from the bleed duct, passes through the hot air pressure regulating valve, and each zone's trim air valve adds the amount needed to reach the target temperature.

question: What happens to the trim air valves when the HOT AIR pushbutton is released (OFF) or a hot air fault occurs?

options.text: The trim air valves open fully
The hot air valve and the trim air valves close, and the zones receive only pack air
The packs shut down automatically
The recirculation fans stop

explanation: Without trim air the packs' temperature alone governs the zones, which is why the cabin may become too cold in some zones.

question: What is the function of the mixer unit?

options.text: To measure the humidity of the air leaving the packs
To mix air from the packs with recirculated cabin air and distribute it to the cockpit and cabin ducts
To mix hot and cold air for the trim air valves
To control cabin pressure

explanation: Recirculated air reduces the fresh air that must be taken from the engines and so saves fuel. The mixer unit takes pack air and recirculated air and feeds the zones.

question: What is the purpose of the recirculation (cabin) fans?

options.text: To cool the avionics equipment
To extract air from the lavatories and galley
To pressurise the cargo compartments
To draw cabin air through filters back into the mixer unit, reducing the bleed air that is needed

explanation: Every kilogram of recirculated air is a kilogram that does not have to be taken from the engine, which is what makes recirculation economical.

question: What does the CAB FANS pushbutton control?

options.text: The cabin recirculation fans
The cargo compartment extraction fans
The avionics bay blower fans
The lavatory and galley extraction fans

explanation: The pushbutton on the overhead panel switches the recirculation fans on or off. They are on in normal operation.

question: Why are recirculation fans switched off in some abnormal situations (such as smoke)?

options.text: To reduce electrical load
To stop the packs from icing
So that smoke or contamination is not drawn around and redistributed through the cabin
To lower the cabin pressure

explanation: Switching them off means the cabin air is made up only from fresh pack air, which is easier to control during smoke procedures.

question: Where does the air for the cockpit zone come from?

options.text: Directly from pack 1 only
From the avionics bay through the skin heat exchanger
From the forward cargo compartment
From the mixer unit through its own duct, with its own trim air valve

explanation: All three zones are fed from the mixer unit; the trim air valves are what make each zone's temperature different.

question: What does the RAM AIR pushbutton do when pressed?

options.text: It closes the ram air inlet flaps of the packs
It opens the emergency ram air inlet so outside air can enter the mixer unit
It increases the pack flow to HI
It opens the outflow valve fully

explanation: The ram air inlet is a last-resort source of ventilation when both packs are lost or the cabin is filled with smoke.

question: What condition is required for the emergency ram air to actually flow into the cabin?

options.text: The pack flow selector must be in HI
The cabin altitude must be above 14 000 ft
The differential pressure must be low (below about 1 psi), otherwise the cabin pressure keeps the ram air valve from admitting air
The APU bleed must be supplying the packs

explanation: Ram air pressure is small. If the cabin is pressurised above that, outside air cannot enter, which is why the cabin must be depressurised (outflow valve open) first.

question: With the RAM AIR pushbutton on and a low differential pressure, what else helps air flow through the cabin?

options.text: The outflow valve opens so the air can leave
The packs go to HI flow
The recirculation fans run faster
The safety valves close

explanation: Air must have a path out of the aircraft as well as in. With cabin pressure at ambient, the outflow valve can open further to let the air pass.

question: What does the ECAM COND page show for each zone?

options.text: The selected target and the actual temperature, together with the duct temperature
The pack inlet pressure and the compressor outlet pressure
The cabin altitude and the differential pressure
The oxygen pressure and the number of passengers

explanation: The COND page lets the crew see how zone temperatures are tracking their selection, and whether a duct temperature is rising towards its limit.

question: Which ECAM page shows the pack outlet temperatures and the pack flows?

options.text: The PRESS page, which carries them beside the cabin altitude
The HYD page, beside the system pressures
The BLEED page, which carries the pack parameters beside the bleed data
The DOOR page, beside the door and slide status

explanation: The pack outlet temperature and flow sit on the BLEED page with the bleed pressures and temperatures. The COND page is about zone and duct temperatures.

question: What does an amber PACK pushbutton FAULT light indicate?

options.text: The pack is switched off by the crew
A pack fault, such as overheat or flow valve disagreement, so the pack is lost or its control is degraded
The pack is operating in HI flow
The cargo ventilation has failed

explanation: FAULT is an automatic indication. The crew then follows the ECAM, which can include selecting the pack off and increasing the flow of the remaining one.

question: Which source supplies the air conditioning packs on the ground with no engines running and the APU not available?

options.text: The packs are supplied by the engines' ground idle bleed
The recirculation fans alone
The emergency ram air inlet
A ground low pressure conditioned-air connection feeds the mixer unit directly

explanation: A low-pressure ground connection delivers conditioned air to the mixer unit, bypassing the packs entirely.

question: Why must the packs be off during the take-off roll in some performance-limited cases?

options.text: Because the packs cannot work on the runway
Because the pack ram air flap is closed on the ground
Because bleed air taken for the packs reduces engine thrust, and turning them off gives a higher take-off performance
Because the recirculation fans would stall

explanation: Bleed extraction costs thrust. A performance-limited take-off may be calculated with packs off, in which case they are switched back on after take-off, once the bleed is no longer a problem.

question: During a normal flight, which bleed source normally feeds the packs after the engines have started?

options.text: The engine bleeds
The APU bleed only
The ground connection
The ram air inlet

explanation: The engines are the normal source in flight. The APU bleed may be used on the ground and in some failure conditions.

question: What is the general role of the secondary channel of the zone controller?

options.text: To control only the cargo compartments
To run only on the ground
To control the packs' ram air flap alone
To take over if the primary channel fails, with less accurate temperature regulation

explanation: The zone controller has two channels so that a single failure does not lose temperature control. If both fail, the pack controllers regulate on fixed default values.
